opening_note: October is San Diego's second summer. Some years the hottest week lands now, when the wind turns and blows in from the desert. But the harvest has moved inland: new dates, new sweet potatoes, heavy pomegranates, the last sweet peppers, and a squash that will sit on your counter until Thanksgiving. For the first time since spring, you can shop for the month instead of the week.
thesis: Keep the meal. Change the season.

month_card.sub: What the desert and the valley send down.

field_notes.name: A new date isn't dried fruit.
field_notes.body: Most dates in the store were picked last fall and have been sitting since. The ones picked this fall are softer, glossier, and taste like caramel instead of candy — squeeze the box and they give. If you ever see yellow dates still on the branch, those are Barhis, eaten crunchy and fresh for a few weeks and nowhere else. Buy a branch.

field_notes.name: October is when peppers go in jars.
field_notes.body: Across the Balkans, autumn is ajvar season: red peppers are at their cheapest, and whole families roast them by the crate and cook them down into a relish that lasts the winter. You don't need a crate. Four peppers and one eggplant make a jar. It's the same impulse behind everything in this basket — buy it while it's here, and make it keep.

field_notes.name: Let the oven cut the kabocha.
field_notes.body: A kabocha is dense enough to be dangerous with a knife. Put it whole in a 400°F oven for ten minutes, or the microwave for three, and the skin softens enough to cut through safely. Don't peel it. Roasted, the skin goes tender and you eat all of it.

field_notes.name: October at the fish counter.
field_notes.body: Rockfish is the local fish that gets more reliable as the water cools: dozens of species, mild and firm, usually cheaper than anything flown in. Ask for it whole. A counter that sells it whole will scale and gut it for you, and a whole fish is easier to cook well than a fillet.

weekend_meal.name: Whole roasted rockfish, and the October salad.
weekend_meal.intro: One meal should feel like the reason you went shopping. In October, it's a whole local fish and a salad that only works this month: the first mild arugula, pomegranate, and new dates.
weekend_meal.card_line: Whole rockfish, arugula, pomegranate, dates, ajvar
ingredients: 1 whole rockfish, 2–3 lbs, scaled and gutted
1 lemon, sliced thin, plus another for the salad
A wedge of parmesan, for shaving
Ajvar and good bread, for the table
weekend_meal.ingredient_note: No whole fish at your counter? Two pounds of rockfish fillets work too — roast them for ten to twelve minutes instead.
weekend_meal.method: Heat the oven to 450°F. Pat the fish dry inside and out and cut three shallow slashes on each side, down to the bone. Rub it all over with olive oil, salt it well, inside and out, and tuck the lemon slices into the cavity. Roast on a sheet pan for 20 to 25 minutes, until the flesh at the thickest part is opaque and pulls easily from the bone. While it roasts, put the arugula, pomegranate, and dates in a wide bowl, but don't dress them. At the table, add olive oil, a squeeze of lemon, and salt, toss, and shave parmesan over the top. Bring the fish out whole. Lift the top fillet off with a spoon, pull out the spine, and serve the bottom fillet. Ajvar and bread on the side.

drink.name: Barrio Logan Jamaica
drink.intro: One drink. It's still hot, and the pomegranates just came in.
drink.method: Cover a cup of dried hibiscus with four cups of cold water and leave it in the fridge overnight — cold-steeped, it comes out bright rather than bitter. Strain. Press the seeds from one pomegranate through a strainer and stir the juice in, with sugar to taste; start with a quarter cup and stop when it's tart-sweet, not sweet. Pour over ice with a squeeze of lime and a spoonful of whole seeds. The pitcher keeps four days.

local_ritual.label: San Diego ritual
local_ritual.name: Go to the desert.
local_ritual.description: Anza-Borrego is two hours east and unbearable until now. October is the first month it isn't. Go for a day, walk until it gets hot, and notice that the dates, the pomegranates, and the citrus coming next all grow somewhere that looks like this — dry, bright, and irrigated. The season in this basket comes from inland, not from the coast.

one_thing_to_notice.headline: The wind from the wrong direction.
one_thing_to_notice.body: A few times each fall the wind turns around and blows from the desert instead of the ocean. The air goes warm and very dry, the sky turns unusually clear, and from the coast you can suddenly see the mountains. It's why October can be hotter than August. When it happens, look east.

kabocha-squash.name: Kabocha squash
kabocha-squash.tile_uses: Rice bowls, tacos, roasted beside anything
kabocha-squash.why_now: Kabocha is the squash that comes after the thin-skinned early ones — dense, dry, and sweeter than butternut. It's picked now and actually improves after a few weeks on the counter, which makes it the first thing in the year you can buy in October and cook in November.
how_to_choose: Dark green, dull rather than shiny — shine means it was picked early
Heavy enough to surprise you
A dry, corky stem
A pale orange patch on one side is fine; that's where it sat on the ground
No soft spots anywhere
kabocha-squash.buy_this_much: 1 large, about 3 lbs. That's two trays of roasted wedges — most of a week of bowls and tacos.
kabocha-squash.price_note: Usually sold by the pound. Cheaper at Asian and Mexican markets than at most supermarkets.

flavor_paths.name: Roasted wedges
flavor_paths.description: Skin on, oil, salt, 425°F until the edges char. The default.

flavor_paths.name: With ajvar
flavor_paths.description: Hot wedges, a spoonful of the jar, arugula on top.

flavor_paths.name: With yogurt
flavor_paths.description: Salted yogurt underneath, pomegranate on top. Sweet, sour, cold, hot.

weekday_uses: Roasted wedges over rice with ajvar
Cubed in tacos with black beans and cotija
Next to salmon on the same sheet pan
Cold, straight from the fridge, with salt
kabocha-squash.weekend_use: A tray of dark-roasted wedges on the table beside the whole fish, for anyone who wants something warm next to the salad.
kabocha-squash.storage: Whole, somewhere cool and dry for up to two months — it gets sweeter over the first few weeks. Once cut, wrap it and refrigerate; use within five days.
kabocha-squash.one_thing_to_learn: Kabocha is drier than other squash, which is why it roasts so well: there's less water to steam off before the sugars can brown. That's also why it can taste chalky if undercooked. Roast it until a knife slides in with no resistance at all, then give it five more minutes.

red-bell-peppers.name: Red bell peppers
red-bell-peppers.tile_uses: The ajvar, eggs, rice bowls, raw with salt
red-bell-peppers.why_now: A red pepper is a green pepper that was left on the plant long enough to ripen, and by the end of the season that's most of what's left. Early fall is when California's red peppers are sweetest and often cheapest. By November they'll be shipped from farther away and priced like it.
how_to_choose: Glossy, firm, and heavy for their size
Deep, even red, with no green shoulders
Thick walls — press gently; they shouldn't flex
A green, fresh-looking stem
Blocky, four-lobed peppers char more evenly than twisted ones
red-bell-peppers.buy_this_much: 6. Four for the jar, two for the week.
red-bell-peppers.price_note: Loose peppers by the pound are almost always cheaper than the packaged three-color bags.

weekday_uses: Charred and cooked down into the ajvar

red-bell-peppers.weekend_use: Charred on Saturday, cooked down into a jar of ajvar that carries the week.
red-bell-peppers.storage: Unwashed in the crisper for a week to ten days. Charred and peeled, four days in the fridge, or freeze the strips flat.
red-bell-peppers.one_thing_to_learn: Green, yellow, and red bell peppers are mostly the same plant at different stages. Red ones have spent the longest ripening, which is why they're sweetest and cost more most of the year. The end of the season is when that extra time is cheap.

sweet-potatoes.name: Sweet potatoes
sweet-potatoes.tile_uses: Tacos, rice bowls, a weeknight dinner on their own
sweet-potatoes.why_now: California's sweet potatoes are dug in September and October, most of them in the Central Valley around Merced, then stored through the winter. The new crop is on shelves now. It's the basket's filling one: a starch that keeps for weeks and makes a dinner on its own.
how_to_choose: Firm from end to end, with no soft or wet tips
Smooth skin, no sprouts or wrinkling
Medium and evenly shaped, so they cook at one speed
Orange-fleshed (garnet or jewel) for roasting
sweet-potatoes.buy_this_much: 2 lbs, about four medium. They keep, so they're the dinner you make when the week gets away from you.
sweet-potatoes.price_note: Cheap now, and cheaper still by the loose pound than in bags.

flavor_paths.name: Roasted in cubes
flavor_paths.description: Small, oiled, 425°F until the edges char. For tacos and bowls.

flavor_paths.name: Baked whole
flavor_paths.description: Split open, salted yogurt, ajvar. A whole dinner in one potato.

flavor_paths.name: With something sharp
flavor_paths.description: Pomegranate or lime over the top. It needs the contrast.

weekday_uses: Roasted cubes in tacos with black beans and cotija
Baked whole, split, with yogurt and a spoonful of ajvar

Roasted cubes under a fried egg
sweet-potatoes.weekend_use: A tray of roasted cubes beside the fish, for anyone who wants something warm and filling.
sweet-potatoes.storage: Somewhere cool and dark, not the fridge — cold makes the centers hard and off-tasting. They keep three weeks or more.
sweet-potatoes.one_thing_to_learn: A baked sweet potato is done well after it's merely soft. Keep going — an hour at 400°F — until the skin puffs away from the flesh and syrup starts to bead out and caramelize on the pan. That's the starch turning to sugar, and it's the difference between a vegetable and a meal.

arugula.name: Arugula
arugula.tile_uses: The salad, pasta, rice bowls, on top of anything
arugula.why_now: Arugula is a cool-weather green. In summer heat it bolts and turns harsh; planted in September, it's ready in October with a gentler, peppery bite. It's the first green in months that tastes like it wanted to grow.
how_to_choose: Bunches with small leaves are milder than big, deeply lobed ones
Perky leaves with no yellowing
No wet or slimy leaves at the bottom of the bag
Bunched arugula from a market usually tastes more of itself than the washed clamshells
arugula.buy_this_much: 2 bunches, or one big bag. Buy it twice a week if you can — it doesn't keep like the rest of this basket.
arugula.price_note: Farmers market bunches are often cheaper per ounce than clamshells, and taste better.

A handful over rice bowls

arugula.weekend_use: The base of the October salad: arugula, pomegranate, and torn dates, dressed at the last second.
arugula.storage: Unwashed, wrapped in a dry paper towel inside a bag, in the crisper. Three or four days. Wash it right before using.
arugula.one_thing_to_learn: Dress greens at the last possible moment. Salt pulls water out of leaves, and oil weighs them down, so a salad dressed ten minutes early is a wilted salad. Put everything in the bowl, carry it to the table, and toss it there.

pomegranates.name: Pomegranates
pomegranates.tile_uses: Over squash, salads, yogurt, the drink
pomegranates.why_now: California grows nearly all of the country's pomegranates, and the harvest runs from late September into November. In October they're heavy, cheap by the piece, and sold everywhere from the farmers market to the corner store. By spring, the only ones left are imported.
how_to_choose: Heavy for its size — weight is juice
Angular and a little lopsided, with flat faces; round ones aren't full yet
Deep red, leathery skin
A small dry crack is fine; a soft or damp spot is not
pomegranates.buy_this_much: 3. One pomegranate gives about a cup of seeds, which is a week of scattering.
pomegranates.price_note: Priced by the piece, so the heaviest one in the bin is the best deal.

pomegranates.weekend_use: Half a pomegranate's seeds in the October salad, next to the whole fish.
pomegranates.storage: Whole, in the fridge for a month or more. Seeded, five days in a covered container.
pomegranates.one_thing_to_learn: To seed one without a mess, score around the crown, pull the fruit apart into sections, and work the seeds loose in a bowl of water. The seeds sink and the white pith floats. Skim, drain, done.
pomegranates.market_question: Which ones came off the tree most recently?

fresh-dates.name: New-crop dates
fresh-dates.tile_uses: Yogurt, the salad, a plate with cheese
fresh-dates.why_now: Nearly every Medjool in the country is grown in the desert two hours from here, in the Coachella and Bard valleys, and they're picked from late summer through October. The ones on shelves now are this year's — soft, glossy, and much better than the ones that have been sitting since last fall.
how_to_choose: Plump and glossy, with skin that clings to the fruit
Soft enough to dent with a thumb
No crystallized sugar on the surface — that's age
A packed-on date printed on the box, if there is one
Yellow dates still on the branch are Barhi: crunchy and fresh, and only around for a few weeks
fresh-dates.buy_this_much: 1 lb. They last for months in the fridge, so this is more about having them than using them up.
fresh-dates.price_note: Costco and Middle Eastern markets are often half the supermarket price for the same Medjools.

fresh-dates.weekend_use: Torn into the October salad, and a small plate of dates, guava, and queso fresco after the fish.
fresh-dates.storage: In the fridge in a closed container for up to six months, or the counter for a few weeks. Cold dates firm up; let them sit out before eating.
fresh-dates.one_thing_to_learn: A date is a fresh fruit that happens to dry well, not a dried fruit. Growers let them cure on the palm in the desert heat, which is why they're soft and sticky rather than leathery. Once you've eaten a new-crop Medjool, you'll notice the difference in the ones that aren't.

guavas.name: Guavas
guavas.tile_uses: Raw with salt and chile, with queso fresco, the drink
guavas.why_now: Guavas ripen in San Diego backyards from late summer into winter, and October is when they fill the bins at Mexican markets and farm stands. Pink-fleshed and fragrant, they're the most tropical thing in a fall basket — a reminder that fall here isn't New England.
how_to_choose: Smell first: a ripe guava is fragrant from a foot away
Pale yellow-green skin, turning from hard green
A slight give when pressed, like a ripe pear
Small brown marks are fine; soft, wet spots are not
guavas.buy_this_much: 5–6. Some ripe now, some firmer for later in the week.
guavas.price_note: Much cheaper at Mexican markets, where they're sold as guayaba.

guavas.storage: On the counter until they're fragrant and give slightly, then in the fridge for three or four days. Their smell travels — keep them in a closed bag.
guavas.one_thing_to_learn: You eat all of a guava: the skin, the flesh, and the small hard seeds. Slice it into rounds and don't bother digging anything out. If the seeds bother you, halve it and scoop the smooth outer flesh, leaving the seedy center for the drink.
